title: Base Conversion
body:
Writing the same number in a different base. Nothing about the value or its
[[Data representation]] changes; only the notation does. The working skill of the course,
because hex is how you read memory and binary is how the machine actually holds it.

The 68000 assembler prefixes tell you which base a literal is written in:

| Prefix | Base | Example | Decimal |
|---|---|---|---|
| `$` | 16, hex | `$FF` | 255 |
| `@` | 8, octal | `@377` | 255 |
| `%` | 2, binary | `%11111111` | 255 |
| *(none)* | 10, decimal | `255` | 255 |

## Converting

**To decimal**: multiply each digit by its place value and add.

```
$2AF = 2×16² + 10×16¹ + 15×16⁰
     = 512 + 160 + 15
     = 687
```

**From decimal**: repeated division, remainders read bottom to top.

```
687 ÷ 16 = 42 r 15   (F)
 42 ÷ 16 =  2 r 10   (A)
  2 ÷ 16 =  0 r  2   (2)
                        → $2AF
```

**Binary to hex** is the one you do by eye, and the reason hex exists: 16 is $2^4$, so every
hex digit is exactly four bits. Group from the right, pad the left with zeros.

```
%1010_1111  →  1010 1111  →  A    F   →  $AF
```

Octal is the same trick with three bits per digit, which is why it is unpopular on a machine
whose word sizes are multiples of four.

## Sizes worth memorising

| Bits | Hex digits | Range (unsigned) | 68000 suffix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 1 | 0–15 | |
| 8 ([[Byte]]) | 2 | 0–255 | `.b` |
| 16 (word) | 4 | 0–65535 | `.w` |
| 32 (longword) | 8 | 0–4294967295 | `.l` |

Signed ranges are the same span shifted: see [[Complements]].
